data:
Lithos talks to three external systems: Roblox legacy site APIs, Roblox
Open Cloud, and (optionally) an S3-compatible bucket for remote state.
Each needs its own credential. None of them are stored or transmitted by
Lithos — they live in environment variables and .env files you control.
Credential	Used for	Required for	ROBLOSECURITY	Legacy Roblox APIs (place uploads, configurations, social links, etc.)	Almost every deploy.	LITHOS_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY	Roblox Open Cloud (asset uploads, place publish, etc.)	Most deploys; required for asset uploads. ROBLOX_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY and MANTLE_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY are also accepted.	LITHOS_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / LITHOS_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY / LITHOS_AWS_INHERIT_IAM_ROLE	S3 / Cloudflare R2 remote state	Only when using remote state.	
Lithos still honors the legacy MANTLE_* names. See
Migrating from Mantle.
data.roblosecurity#ROBLOSECURITY:
This is the same browser cookie Roblox uses to keep you logged in to
roblox.com and Roblox Studio. Lithos prefers
not to require you to extract it manually:
If you are signed in to Roblox Studio on this machine, Lithos picks
the cookie up from the OS keychain (Windows Credential Manager / macOS
Keychain). Nothing for you to do.
If not, set it explicitly:
export ROBLOSECURITY="…"
$env:ROBLOSECURITY = "…"
Or add it to a .env file at the project root.
A ROBLOSECURITY cookie is the equivalent of your Roblox password.
Never commit it to Git. Add .env to .gitignore. Rotate it
immediately if it leaks (Account → Security → Sign out of all sessions).
data.extracting-the-cookie-manually#Extractin:
If automatic detection does not find your cookie (common on headless CI
or new machines):
Sign in to roblox.com in any modern browser.
Open DevTools → Application → Cookies → https://www.roblox.com.
Copy the value of the .ROBLOSECURITY cookie.
In CI, store it as a secret named ROBLOSECURITY.
data.lithos_open_cloud_api_key-preferred#LITH:
Roblox Open Cloud is the modern, scoped, server-to-server API. You will
want a key for almost every project:
Go to the Creator Hub credentials page.
Create a new API key.
Add the experiences this project deploys to under Access Permissions.
Grant the operations Lithos needs:
universe-places:write — for publishing places.
asset:read, asset:write — for uploading image and audio assets.
Optionally restrict the key by IP. CI runners often have stable
egress IPs you can pin.
Set the key.
Example .env entry:
LITHOS_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY="…"
Lithos also accepts ROBLOX_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY and the legacy
MANTLE_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY, but LITHOS_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY is the
preferred name for docs and CI.Deploy preflight now introspects this key before apply when possible. If the
key is missing, lacks universe-places.write, or is scoped to the wrong
universe, Lithos stops early and prints the likely cause plus next steps.
data.aws-credentials-only-for-remote-state#AW:
If you use remote state, Lithos needs S3 (or R2,
or any S3-compatible) credentials with Get / Put / List on the state
prefix.
LITHOS_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID="…"
LITHOS_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="…"
For workloads running on AWS infrastructure (EC2 instance profiles, ECS
task roles, EKS service accounts), set:
LITHOS_AWS_INHERIT_IAM_ROLE=1
and Lithos will pick up the ambient role instead of looking for explicit
keys.R2-specific configuration (account ID, endpoint, scope) is documented on
Cloudflare R2 remote state.
data.using-a-env-file#Using a .env file:
Lithos automatically loads a .env file from the project root and from
the current working directory. The file is dotenv-format
(KEY="value" per line, # comments). This is the recommended way to
hold secrets locally:If you invoke Lithos from outside the project, for example
lithos outputs path/to/project, it still loads the .env next to the
resolved project config in addition to any .env in the current working
directory.
ROBLOSECURITY="…"
LITHOS_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY="…"

# Only if using remote state
LITHOS_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID="…"
LITHOS_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="…"
.env
.env.*
Never check .env in. The same file in CI should be replaced by
encrypted secrets injected as real environment variables.

data.what-you-can-override-per-environment#Wh:
Each entry under environments accepts the following keys (all optional):
Key	Effect	label	Identifier you pass to --environment. Required.	branches	Restrict this environment to specific Git branches. CI uses this.	targetAccess	Override visibility for this environment. private, friends, or public.	targetNamePrefix	Prefix the experience and place names. See below.	targetOverrides	Arbitrary deep merge into target for this environment.

Getting Started — try a real two-environment
deploy.
Continuous deployment — lock prod
behind CI on main.

data:
Internally, Lithos models your project as a directed acyclic graph of
resources. Every individual thing Roblox exposes — an experience, a
place, a place's configuration, a developer product, a thumbnail — is one
node. Edges encode "this resource needs that resource's outputs to exist
before it can be created."You will rarely look at the graph directly, but understanding the model
explains every behaviour you'll see in the CLI output.
data.a-resource-has-four-parts#A resource has:
Part	Description	Type	What kind of Roblox thing it is (place, developerProduct, thumbnail, …).	ID	A stable identifier within your project, e.g. place_start. Lithos generates these from your config.	Inputs	The fields you set in lithos.yml plus the outputs of resources it depends on.	Outputs	What Roblox returned after creating it (asset IDs, version numbers, …). Outputs feed the inputs of dependent resources.	
A change is any difference between a resource's persisted inputs and its
freshly-computed inputs. Lithos uses this to decide between
create, update, noop, and delete.
data.how-a-deploy-unfolds#How a deploy unfold:
1. Load lithos.yml + state file
read-only
2. Live reconciliation pass
verify experiences, places, products, passes
against the Roblox API
3. Build the desired graph from config
read-only
4. Diff desired vs. reconciled state
render plan preview
read-only
5. Confirm (interactive) / auto-approve (CI)
then apply in dependency order
apply phase
6. Write new state
commit
Steps 1–4 are read-only (green). Nothing on Roblox changes until you
confirm at step 5 (amber). This is what makes destructive mistakes
recoverable: you always see them coming.
The diagram is intentionally simplified. Current deploy runs a preflight
diagnostics pass before confirmation, writes a rollback checkpoint before
apply, and saves both the new current graph and deployment journal to
state afterward.
data.operation-kinds#Operation kinds:
Each node in the diff is exactly one of these:
+ create — exists in config, not in state.
~ update — exists in both, inputs differ.
− delete — exists in state, not in config.
= noop — inputs match. No API call.
↷ skip — its dependencies failed; cannot proceed.
In CI logs you will see lines like:
Succeeded with 0 create(s), 1 update(s), 0 delete(s), 5 noop(s), 0 skip(s)
That summary is the only number that matters when reviewing a deploy in
hindsight: a deploy with 0 delete(s) and 0 skip(s) was fully successful
and non-destructive.
data.why-deletes-are-never-silent#Why deletes:
If you remove a resource from lithos.yml, the next deploy will plan a
delete. That is by design — the YAML is the source of truth, and the
absence of a resource means delete it.What is not silent:
The plan preview marks the destructive operation with an explicit
warning before any API call.
In an interactive terminal, Lithos prompts for confirmation. Cancel, and
nothing happens.
In CI, deletes are still applied (otherwise you could never decommission
anything from a pipeline), but they are clearly logged.
Deletes from a Lithos perspective are also archives from a Roblox
perspective. Roblox does not generally permit hard-deleting assets, so
Lithos archives them and removes them from state. They will not come back
on the next deploy unless you re-add them to your config.
data.drift-and-what-lithos-does-about-it#Drif:
If someone — a teammate, a moderator, your past self — changes a Roblox
resource through the Creator Hub or Studio, the state file no longer
matches reality. Lithos calls that drift.During the live reconciliation pass (step 2 above), Lithos asks Roblox to
confirm that each resource it thinks exists actually exists, classifying
each one:
verified — Roblox confirmed it. Use the persisted state as-is.
missing — Roblox said it does not exist. Drop it from state so the
next plan re-creates it.
skipped — no cheap, authoritative existence check (e.g. thumbnails).
Trust the persisted state.
unknown — the API call itself failed (network, permission). Trust
the persisted state to fail safe.
The net effect: if a place gets deleted in the dashboard, the next deploy
re-creates it instead of producing a broken update against a non-existent
asset. If the API is flaky, Lithos does not destroy your state.

data:
The state file is how Lithos remembers what it created. Without it, every
deploy would have to re-discover every asset on Roblox, and there is no
generic API for "list everything I own." With it, a deploy is a fast,
predictable diff.
data.what-is-in-the-state-file#What is in the:
A versioned YAML document keyed by environment. In the current v7 format,
each environment stores two things:
current — the resource graph from the latest successful deploy or undo.
deployments — a short history of checkpoints, results, and journals used
for recovery and lithos undo.
Concretely:
version: 7
environments:
  dev:
    current:
      - id: experience_singleton
        inputs:
          experience:
            groupId: ~
        outputs:
          experience:
            assetId: 3296599132
            startPlaceId: 8667346609
      - id: placeFile_start
        inputs:
          placeFile:
            filePath: game.rbxlx
            fileHash: 0c3a…
        outputs:
          placeFile:
            version: 2
    deployments:
      - id: deploy-1736370930123
        kind: deploy
        status: succeeded
        startedAt: 2026-01-08T01:15:30Z
        finishedAt: 2026-01-08T01:15:42Z
        baseline: []
        desired:
          - id: experience_singleton
        resulting:
          - id: experience_singleton
        journal:
          - resourceId: experience_singleton
            action: create
            status: applied
            summary: Applied create for experience_singleton
You will rarely edit this by hand. The two things you should know:
fileHash is how Lithos decides if a place file changed. Editing
game.rbxlx flips the hash, which produces an update. Touching the file
without changing bytes does not.
outputs.assetId is the canonical link between a Lithos resource and
a real Roblox asset. Lose it and the next deploy will re-create the
asset from scratch.
deployments is the recovery trail. It records the last few deploys and
undos, including the baseline snapshot and a short journal of what changed.
lithos undo uses that history rather than guessing from Git.
data.where-the-state-file-lives#Where the sta:
Two options. They produce identical state; only the storage backend
differs. Both include the same current graph and rollback history.
data.local-the-default#Local (the default):
.lithos-state.yml is written next to your lithos.yml. Commit it.Local state is fine when:
You are the only developer.
You only deploy from one machine.
You are happy to merge state-file conflicts in Git when collaborators
deploy from different branches.
data.remote-s3-r2#Remote (S3, R2):
State is written to a single object in S3 or Cloudflare R2. Multiple
machines see the same state automatically.Remote state is the right answer when:
More than one person, machine, or CI job deploys.
You want CI to be the only thing that deploys to prod, with developers
deploying to dev from their laptops.
You don't want a state file in source control.
Setup: Remote state guide.
There is no third option. Lithos does not do "no state" — that would mean
re-creating every resource on every deploy. Pick local or remote.
data.drift-in-one-paragraph#Drift, in one par:
Drift is when the live Roblox state and the Lithos state file disagree.
Most commonly it happens because somebody changed something through the
Creator Hub or Studio. Lithos's live reconciliation pass detects drift
for the resource types it can cheaply verify (experiences, places, game
passes, developer products) and updates state to match reality before
planning the diff. See The resource graph.You can run the reconciliation pass on its own without applying anything:
$ lithos diff --live
That prints the same diff a deploy would, against the reconciled state,
without prompting and without writing.
data.legacy-mantleyml--mantle-stateyml#Legacy:
Lithos transparently reads both Mantle and Lithos config and state files.
On any new write, Lithos always uses the Lithos-named files. There is no
flag day; Mantle projects can be migrated incrementally. See
Migrating from Mantle.
data.common-state-file-questions#Common state:
Q: My teammate and I both deployed dev and now Git can't merge the
state file.
You either need remote state, or you need a convention where only one
machine deploys dev (often: only CI). The state file is not designed
for parallel writers.Q: Can I delete the state file and start over?
Yes, but Lithos will think nothing exists and try to re-create every
resource. The old assets stay on Roblox, orphaned, and you lose the rollback
checkpoints recorded in deployments. Better: use
lithos import to attach an existing experience to a fresh state file
(experimental).Q: Can I edit the state file by hand?
Technically yes. Practically: only ever as a last resort, and always make
a backup first. The outputs section is what binds Lithos to Roblox
asset IDs — if you change an assetId to one you do not own, the next
deploy will fail authentication; if you change it to one someone else
owns, you may inadvertently mutate an asset you are not entitled to.
data.continue-with#Continue with:
Environments — how one config file
produces multiple isolated state graphs.
Remote state — set up S3 or R2 state.

data:
The endgame for any infrastructure-as-code tool is "PR merges, deploy
runs, done." This page sketches a minimal CI setup for Lithos using
GitHub Actions. The same pattern applies to GitLab CI, Buildkite,
CircleCI, Jenkins, etc.Two things make this setup robust:
Remote state. With state in S3 or R2, every CI run sees the same
previous-state, deployment checkpoints, and rollback history regardless of
which runner picked it up. Without remote state, two runners can race and
produce divergent state files.
Branch-gated environments. A prod environment that only deploys
from main cannot be deployed by a pull request, no matter how the
workflow file is written.
data.prerequisites#Prerequisites:
Remote state configured for the project.
An Open Cloud API key with the right scopes — see
Authentication.
A ROBLOSECURITY cookie with permission to manage the experiences
this project owns.
A lithos.yml whose prod environment has branches: [main]:
environments:
  - label: dev
    targetNamePrefix: environmentLabel
    branches: [develop]
  - label: prod
    targetAccess: public
    branches: [main]
{
  "environments": [
    {
      "label": "dev",
      "targetNamePrefix": "environmentLabel",
      "branches": [
        "develop"
      ]
    },
    {
      "label": "prod",
      "targetAccess": "public",
      "branches": [
        "main"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
data.secrets#Secrets:
Add four repository secrets (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions):
Secret	Value	ROBLOSECURITY	Your Roblox cookie.	LITHOS_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY	Your Open Cloud key.	LITHOS_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID	S3 / R2 access key.	LITHOS_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY	S3 / R2 secret.	
Use LITHOS_* in new CI and team docs so your workflow matches the current
examples. Legacy MANTLE_* variables are still accepted for compatibility.
data.a-minimal-workflow#A minimal workflow:
name: Deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, develop]
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Install Foreman
        uses: Roblox/setup-foreman@v1
        with:
          token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Pick environment
        id: env
        run: |
          if [ "${GITHUB_REF}" = "refs/heads/main" ]; then
            echo "label=prod" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "label=dev" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          fi

      - name: Deploy
        env:
          ROBLOSECURITY: ${{ secrets.ROBLOSECURITY }}
          LITHOS_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.LITHOS_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY }}
          LITHOS_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.LITHOS_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}
          LITHOS_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: ${{ secrets.LITHOS_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}
        run: lithos deploy --environment ${{ steps.env.outputs.label }} --plain-preview
A few details worth understanding:
--plain-preview drops ANSI color codes from the plan preview so
GitHub's log viewer renders them legibly. Lithos auto-approves when
stdout is not a TTY, so no --yes flag is needed.
Preflight diagnostics run before apply even in CI. Missing Open Cloud
scopes, wrong universe access, and other known deploy blockers fail the job
before any mutation is attempted.
The branch → environment mapping in the script is a belt-and-suspenders
measure on top of the branches: constraint in lithos.yml. Either
alone would prevent a develop push from touching prod, but both is
more obvious to a future reader.
Foreman pins the Lithos version via foreman.toml. This is important:
CI should not silently pick up a new Lithos release the day it's
published.
If a deploy finishes in a bad state, run lithos undo --environment <label>
--plain-preview against the same remote state backend. Because the state file
contains recent checkpoints, rollback can be initiated from a runner or an
operator workstation without reconstructing an older YAML revision first.
data.pull-request-previews#Pull-request previ:
A common companion workflow: on every PR, run lithos diff --live and
post the output as a comment. That way reviewers see "this PR will create
2 places, update 1 game pass, delete 0 resources" without anything having
to be applied.
name: Diff

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main, develop]

jobs:
  diff:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: Roblox/setup-foreman@v1
        with:
          token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Diff
        env:
          ROBLOSECURITY: ${{ secrets.ROBLOSECURITY }}
          LITHOS_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.LITHOS_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY }}
          LITHOS_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.LITHOS_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}
          LITHOS_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: ${{ secrets.LITHOS_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}
        run: lithos diff --environment dev --live --plain-preview
--live also surfaces drift introduced by hand-edits to the Creator Hub,
which is exactly the moment you want to know about it.

data:
This page takes you from zero to a deployed Roblox experience in about ten
minutes. By the end you will have:
The lithos binary installed and on your PATH.
A working Roblox Open Cloud API key and a ROBLOSECURITY cookie.
A deployed dev environment created from the
getting-started example.
A working mental model of what just happened.
If you have never used Lithos before, read
What is Lithos? first — it is short, and the rest of this
guide assumes that vocabulary.
data.prerequisites#Prerequisites:
Git. Install it if you do not have it.
A terminal that handles UTF-8. PowerShell, Windows Terminal, macOS
Terminal, and any modern Linux terminal are fine. Legacy cmd.exe will
garble Lithos's box-drawing output.
A Roblox account that owns the experiences you will manage. Lithos
cannot deploy to experiences you do not own.
data.1-install-lithos#1. Install Lithos:
The recommended path is Foreman — a
Roblox toolchain manager that pins tool versions per-project. The
Installation page walks through Foreman setup
in detail; the short version:
Download the latest foreman-x.x.x-win64.zip from the
Foreman releases page
and extract foreman.exe somewhere stable (e.g. C:\Programs\foreman\).
Add that folder and %USERPROFILE%\.foreman\bin to your PATH.
In a new PowerShell window, verify:
foreman --version
Download the latest foreman-x.x.x-macos.zip (or -linux.zip) from
Foreman releases and
move the extracted binary onto your PATH (e.g. /usr/local/bin/).
Add ~/.foreman/bin to your PATH in your shell rc.
Verify:
foreman --version
Now clone the example repo and let Foreman install Lithos:
git clone https://github.com/siriuslatte/lithos
cd lithos/examples
foreman install
lithos --version
The version you get is whatever examples/foreman.toml pins.
If you would rather grab a prebuilt binary directly, see the
Installation page.
data.2-authenticate#2. Authenticate:
The example deploys to a real Roblox account, so Lithos needs two things:
A ROBLOSECURITY cookie (used for the legacy site APIs).
A LITHOS_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY (used for everything Open Cloud supports;
ROBLOX_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY is also accepted).
The Authentication page has the full story.
The shortest version:
Get an Open Cloud API key from the Creator Hub.
Grant it universe-places:write, asset:read, and asset:write for
the experiences you'll manage.
If you are signed in to Roblox Studio on this machine, Lithos will pick
up your ROBLOSECURITY automatically. If not, set it explicitly.
Put both in a .env file at the project root (next to examples/),
and add .env to .gitignore.
Example .env:
LITHOS_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY="…"
ROBLOSECURITY="…"
data.3-deploy#3. Deploy:
From examples/:
$ lithos deploy projects/getting-started --environment dev
Lithos prints several sections: Loading project,
Running preflight checks, Checkpointing deployment state,
Deploying resources, and Saving state, followed by a summary of where
the new experience lives on Roblox.
Loading project:
  ╷
  │  Loaded config file projects/getting-started/lithos.yml
  │  Selected provided environment configuration dev
  │  Loading previous state from local file projects/getting-started/.lithos-state.yml
  │  No previous state for environment dev
  │
  ╰─ Succeeded
That block is your audit trail: which config Lithos loaded, which
environment it selected, where it looked for previous state, what it
found.The next block is the diff Lithos plans to apply. On a fresh deploy
everything is a create:
Deploying resources:
  ╷
  │  + Creating: experience_singleton
  │    ╷
  │    │  Dependencies:
  │    │      []
  │    │  Inputs:
  │    │    + experience:
  │    │    +   groupId: ~
  │    │
  │    ╰─ Succeeded with outputs:
  │         + experience:
  │         +   assetId: 3296599132
  │         +   startPlaceId: 8667346609

... cut for brevity ...

  │
  ╰─ Succeeded with 6 create(s), 0 update(s), 0 delete(s), 0 noop(s), 0 skip(s)
The summary line is the part you want to scan in CI logs:
6 create(s), 0 delete(s) means six resources were created and nothing
was destroyed.If preflight finds a blocking issue first — a missing Open Cloud key, wrong
universe scope, or an unsupported target-access setting — Lithos stops before
mutating anything and prints the likely cause plus next steps.Finally:
Target results:
  ╷
  │  Experience:
  │    https://www.roblox.com/games/8667346609
  │
  │  Places:
  │    start: https://www.roblox.com/games/8667346609
  │
  ╰──○
Open the link to launch your new experience.
data.5-undo-a-bad-deploy#5. Undo a bad deploy:
$ lithos undo projects/getting-started --environment dev
undo imports the live experience, loads the last checkpoint Lithos recorded
for that environment, previews the diff back to that checkpoint, and then
applies it. This is best-effort rather than transactional, but it is much
faster than manually rebuilding state after a bad push.
data.6-optional-clean-up#6. (Optional) clean:
If you do not want the example experience hanging around your account:
$ lithos destroy projects/getting-started --environment dev
Roblox does not allow hard-deletes for most asset types, so "destroy"
means archived and removed from Lithos state.
data.what-to-read-next#What to read next:
The resource graph — what 5 noop(s)
actually meant, and how the +/~/− markers are decided.
State and reconciliation — what
.lithos-state.yml is for and when to make it remote.
Environments — how dev and prod
share a config without overwriting each other.
CLI reference — every subcommand and flag.
Configuration reference — every
field in lithos.yml.

data:
Lithos is a continuation of Mantle.
The mental model, CLI surface, and config schema are intentionally the same;
the binary, file names, and environment variables have been renamed, and a
number of bugs and limitations have been fixed along the way.You do not need to do a flag-day migration. Lithos transparently reads
Mantle-named files and environment variables, so an existing project keeps
working the moment you swap the binary. This guide walks through the
changes and the recommended order in which to adopt them.
data.renames-at-a-glance#Renames at a glance: Mantle	Lithos	Compatibility	mantle binary	lithos binary	Same subcommands, same flags.	mantle.yml / mantle.yaml	lithos.yml / lithos.yaml / lithos.json	All are read; discovery checks lithos.yml, then lithos.yaml, then lithos.json, then legacy mantle.yml, mantle.yaml.	.mantle-state.yml	.lithos-state.yml	Both are read; lithos-named wins. New writes always go to the Lithos name.	<key>.mantle-state.yml (S3/R2)	<key>.lithos-state.yml	Same fallback for remote keys.	MANTLE_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY	LITHOS_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY	Both honored; LITHOS_* wins. ROBLOX_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY is also accepted.	MANTLE_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID	LITHOS_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID	Both honored; LITHOS_* wins.	MANTLE_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY	LITHOS_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY	Both honored; LITHOS_* wins.	MANTLE_AWS_INHERIT_IAM_ROLE	LITHOS_AWS_INHERIT_IAM_ROLE	Both honored.
data.whats-different-beyond-the-rename#What's:
Things Lithos does that Mantle does not. Most of these are quality-of-life
fixes; some are new capabilities.
Live reconciliation against the Roblox API. Before applying a deploy,
Lithos verifies that the experiences, places, game passes, and developer
products it thinks exist actually exist. Resources deleted in the
Creator Hub are dropped from state and re-created instead of producing
a broken update. See The resource graph.
Plan preview before apply. Every deploy shows a structured,
field-level diff before any API call. Destructive operations on
developer products, game passes, badges, notifications, experiences, and
places are flagged explicitly. Cancel before confirmation and nothing
happens. See CLI reference.
Preflight diagnostics and rollback checkpoints. Lithos validates the
common Roblox failure modes before apply, stores the previous environment
graph as a checkpoint, and provides lithos undo for best-effort recovery.
lithos diff --live. Run the same reconciliation pass that deploy
runs, but only print the diff — useful for "what would happen if I
deployed right now?" without prompting or writing.
Cloudflare R2 remote state. Lithos talks to any S3-compatible
endpoint, including R2. See Cloudflare R2 remote state.
Better CI ergonomics. Auto-approves when stdout is not a TTY,
--plain-preview for log viewers without ANSI support, --no-preview
for fast pipelines that already trust their inputs.
Honest error messages. Several Mantle log lines that referenced the
wrong credential type (e.g. claiming MANTLE_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY was a
ROBLOSECURITY) have been corrected.
data.recommended-migration-order#Recommended:
You can do all of this in a single PR, or stretch it over several. Each
step is independently safe.
data.2-run-a-deploy#2. Run a deploy:
$ lithos deploy --environment dev
You will see a warning: line if Lithos picks up a mantle.yml,
mantle.yaml, if it finds multiple discovered project configs and has to
apply its precedence rule, or
.mantle-state.yml. The deploy itself proceeds normally. After it
completes, a fresh .lithos-state.yml is written next to (not replacing)
the legacy file.
data.3-rename-the-config-file#3. Rename the c:
Rename mantle.yml → lithos.yml or mantle.yaml → lithos.yaml.
If you prefer JSON, convert the config and save it as lithos.json.
Lithos prefers lithos.yml, then lithos.yaml, then lithos.json, and
prefers any of those over the legacy Mantle names; renaming silences the
legacy-file warning.
data.4-update-environment-variables#4. Update:
In your CI secrets, in your .env files, and in your team docs, replace
the MANTLE_* variables with LITHOS_* when convenient. Both work; LITHOS_* is
preferred and ROBLOX_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY is also accepted as an alias.
- MANTLE_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY="…"
- MANTLE_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID="…"
- MANTLE_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="…"
+ LITHOS_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY="…"
+ LITHOS_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID="…"
+ LITHOS_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="…"
data.5-delete-the-legacy-state-files#5. Delet:
Once you have verified that the new .lithos-state.yml (or remote object)
is correct and a deploy applied cleanly against it, delete the legacy
.mantle-state.yml file or the legacy <key>.mantle-state.yml object in
your bucket.
Do not delete the legacy state file before running at least one
successful Lithos deploy. The legacy file is your rollback path while
you verify the migration. After that first Lithos deploy, the new
.lithos-state.yml will also contain Lithos-managed rollback checkpoints.
data.what-does-not-change#What does not chang:
The config schema. Every key valid in mantle.yml or mantle.yaml is
valid in lithos.yml, lithos.yaml, and lithos.json. The configuration reference
is the same shape Mantle had, with later additions.
The state-file format. A Mantle state file is a Lithos state file with a
different name.
The set of supported Roblox resources.
Authentication: same ROBLOSECURITY cookie, same Open Cloud API key.
data.help-my-deploy-errors-out-after-migratio:
A few things to check:
Are both env-var names set? During the transition, having both
MANTLE_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY and LITHOS_OPEN_CLOUD_API_KEY set is fine;
LITHOS_* wins.
Is the state file actually being read? The "Loading project" block
in the deploy output names the file. If it says
.mantle-state.yml, no .lithos-state.yml was found. This is normal
the first time.
Are remote state credentials still valid? LITHOS_AWS_* credentials
need the same permissions on the same bucket as the MANTLE_AWS_* ones
they replace.
Does the legacy CI environment still source a MANTLE_* variable
that overrides the new one? Lithos prefers LITHOS_* if both are
set in the same scope, but a stale shell hook can still surprise you.
If something else is going wrong, please open an issue.

data:
Foreman is a toolchain manager for Roblox tools. You can
configure Foreman to install Lithos with the following foreman.toml config:
[tools]
lithos = { source = "siriuslatte/lithos", version = "<version>" }
You can check for the latest Lithos version on the
releases page.This is the recommended method as it enables consistent version management across your team,
provides better interop with other tools, and makes using Lithos in CI environments (especially
GitHub Action) simpler.If you need help installing Foreman, check out the Getting Started
guide.You can download prebuilt binaries from the latest
release.

Lithos saves the state of your resources in state files which enables it to make only the required
changes to your resources after your configuration and files change.By default, Lithos will save your state to a local .lithos-state.yml file which you can check-in
to your Git repo. But Lithos can also save your state to remote files stored in a cloud provider
which comes with a few benefits.Since a remote state file can be accessed and updated from anywhere, you can share it across
branches and computers. This makes it less likely your state files gets out of sync with the real
resources in Roblox, and it is ideal for continuous deployment (CD) scenarios.Remote state now carries more than the latest resource graph. It also stores a
short deployment history per environment, including rollback checkpoints and
apply journals. That means a CI runner and a local operator looking at the
same remote object also see the same recovery history for lithos undo.

data.create-an-account#Create an account:
In order to create an AWS account you will need to provide a credit card. Amazon S3 provides a
generous free tier which you are very unlikely to reach the limits of while using Lithos, but you
should always monitor your usage to make sure you do not incur unexpected costs.Create an AWS account from their sign up page.
data.create-an-s3-bucket#Create an S3 bucket:
From the AWS console, click the search bar at the top of the page and search for "S3" and select the
S3 service.From the "Buckets" tab, click the "Create bucket" button. Give your bucket a name like
{your-name}-lithos-states and select an AWS region that is near your location. Ensure "Block all
public access" is checked to keep your data private.In the future, Lithos may support object locking, so you may want to expand "Advanced settings" and
enable "Object lock" so that you will not need to re-create your bucket later.Click "Create bucket" to finish creating your bucket.
data.upload-your-existing-state-file#Upload y:
If you are migrating an existing project from local state files to remote, you will need to upload
your state file to your bucket.Before you do so though you need to pick your project name which will be used for the name of the
state file in your bucket and in your Lithos configuration in the next step.Rename your local state file to {project-name}.lithos-state.yml, then upload it to your bucket.
From the S3 buckets tab, click on your new bucket's name, then click the "Upload" button. Click "Add
files" and open your renamed state file. Click "Upload" to finish uploading the state file.
data.configure-your-lithos-project#Configure:
Head back to your Lithos config file and add the state configuration:
# ...your existing configuration
state:
  remote:
    region: [<aws-region>]
    bucket: <bucket-name>
    key: <project-name>
{
  "state": {
    "remote": {
      "region": [
        "<aws-region>"
      ],
      "bucket": "<bucket-name>",
      "key": "<project-name>"
    }
  }
}
Replace <aws-region> with the region you selected when you created your bucket (e.g.
us-west-2).
Replace <bucket-name> with the name you selected when you created your bucket.
Replace <project-name> with the name of your project. This will be used to name the state file
in your bucket. For example, if you supply pirate-wars it will create a
pirate-wars.lithos-state.yml file in your bucket.
data.supply-your-aws-credentials#Supply your:
At this point if you were to run lithos deploy it would attempt to download your state file from
S3 but it would fail because you have not provided any authorization for your bucket.You can read the Authentication guide for
information on supplying your AWS credentials.Once supplied, you can run lithos deploy or any other commands and they will operate on your
remote state file! If you were migrating from local state to remote state, you should delete the
.lithos-state.yml file from your Git repo as it will be unused and out of date.

data:
Cloudflare R2 is an S3-compatible object storage service. You can configure Lithos's S3 provider to
use Cloudflare R2.
data.create-an-account#Create an account: Create a Cloudflare account from their sign up page.
data.create-an-r2-bucket#Create an R2 bucket:
From the Cloudflare console, select R2 from the sidebar and click "Create bucket." Give your bucket a name
like {your-name}-lithos-states. By default, access is restricted so only you can access your data.Click "Create bucket" to finish creating your bucket.
data.upload-your-existing-state-file#Upload y:
If you are migrating an existing project from local state files to remote, you will need to upload
your state file to your bucket.Before you do so though you need to pick your project name which will be used for the name of the
state file in your bucket and in your Lithos configuration in the next step.Rename your local state file to {project-name}.lithos-state.yml, then upload it to your bucket. From the
Cloudflare bucket console, drag and drop your state file or open the file picker to upload your file.
data.configure-your-lithos-project#Configure:
Head back to your Lithos config file and add the state configuration:
# ...your existing configuration
state:
  remote:
    region:
      custom:
        name: <r2-region-name>
        endpoint: <r2-s3-api>
    bucket: <bucket-name>
    key: <project-name>
{
  "state": {
    "remote": {
      "region": {
        "custom": {
          "name": "<r2-region-name>",
          "endpoint": "<r2-s3-api>"
        }
      },
      "bucket": "<bucket-name>",
      "key": "<project-name>"
    }
  }
}
Replace <r2-region-name> with the region your bucket was created in. This will generally be the closest
region to yourself or the region you specified during creation. Check the R2
docs for the full list of
possible regions.
Replace <r2-s3-api> with the API endpoint for your bucket. You can find this in your bucket's settings tab
under the "Bucket Details" section.
Replace <bucket-name> with the name you selected when you created your bucket.
Replace <project-name> with the name of your project. This will be used to name the state file
in your bucket. For example, if you supply pirate-wars it will create a
pirate-wars.lithos-state.yml file in your bucket.
data.supply-your-r2-credentials#Supply your R:
At this point if you were to run lithos deploy it would attempt to download your state file from
R2 but it would fail because you have not provided any authorization for your bucket.To get your credentials, go to the R2 Overview page on Cloudflare, and navigate to "Manage R2 API Tokens".
Create a new token with the "Object Read & Write" permissions and apply it to your bucket. Once created, you
will see a couple of secrets. You'll need to use the "Access Key ID" and "Secret Access Key" for Lithos.To learn how to pass these credentials to Lithos, read the
Authentication guide.Once supplied, you can run lithos deploy or any other commands and they will operate on your
remote state file! If you were migrating from local state to remote state, you should delete the
.lithos-state.yml file from your Git repo as it will be unused and out of date.

data:
Every Lithos workflow is one of six subcommands. This page is the working
reference; for the full machine-readable surface, run lithos --help or
lithos <subcommand> --help.
Command	Purpose	deploy	Reconcile state with config and apply the diff.	diff	Print the diff without applying it.	undo	Restore the last recorded checkpoint for an environment.	outputs	Print the outputs of the last deploy as JSON, YAML, or importable modules.	destroy	Remove every resource Lithos manages for an environment.	import	Adopt an existing experience into a Lithos project.	
All commands accept a positional PROJECT argument. If omitted, Lithos
looks for lithos.yml, then lithos.yaml, then the legacy mantle.yml
and mantle.yaml in the current directory; if provided as a directory,
Lithos looks inside it; if provided as a file, Lithos uses that file
directly. See
Configuration → Config file resolution.
data.deploy#deploy:
$ lithos deploy [PROJECT] --environment <label> [flags]
The default workflow. deploy runs the pipeline described in
The resource graph:
load config and state, reconcile state against the live Roblox API, build
the desired graph, run preflight diagnostics, render a plan preview, prompt
for confirmation, checkpoint the current environment state, and apply the diff
in dependency order.
data.live-reconciliation#Live reconciliation:
Before computing any diff, deploy asks Roblox to confirm that the
resources persisted in state still exist. Each resource is classified as
verified, missing, skipped, or unknown. Resources confirmed
missing are dropped from the previous-state graph so the next plan
re-creates them rather than producing a broken update against a deleted
asset. Resources whose verification is inconclusive (permission denied,
network error) are preserved unchanged so behavior degrades safely.Verified resource types: experiences, places, game passes, developer
products. Sub-resources (configurations, thumbnails, ordering, place files,
badges, image/audio assets, asset aliases, social links, spatial voice,
notifications) are skipped intentionally — they have no cheap, authoritative
existence endpoint, and their drift is implied by the verification of
their parent.
data.plan-preview-and-confirmation#Plan previ:
Before any creates, updates, or deletes hit Roblox, deploy renders a
plan preview: a color-coded, structured view of every operation,
grouped by kind. Risky resources (developer products, game passes,
badges) get field-level summaries — price, name, description — so you
can confirm an "update" really is just a price change before approving
it. Destructive operations on developer products, game passes, badges,
notifications, experiences, and places are flagged with an explicit
warning marker.When stdout is an interactive terminal, deploy prompts to confirm before
applying. Press y or Enter to apply; anything else cancels. In
non-interactive contexts (CI, piped output) deploy auto-approves after
printing a plain summary, so existing scripts continue to work.
data.preflight-diagnostics-and-checkpoints#Pr:
Before approval, deploy runs a preflight pass over the plan and auth
context. This catches the common Roblox failures that are otherwise vague at
runtime: missing Open Cloud keys, missing universe-places.write, API keys
that do not cover the target universe, unsupported group/public/friends
combinations, and place files that are close to Roblox's size limits.If any preflight diagnostic is blocking, deploy stops before mutating
anything. If preflight passes, Lithos records a checkpoint of the last known
good graph so lithos undo can roll the environment back toward that
snapshot later.
data.useful-flags#Useful flags:
Flag	Effect	--environment <label> / -e	Required. Which environment block to apply.	--yes / -y	Skip the confirmation prompt and apply immediately.	--no-preview	Skip the preview entirely. Implies --yes.	--plain-preview	Render a plain (non-colored) summary. Useful in CI log viewers without ANSI support.	--allow-purchases	Allow paid-asset operations (developer products, etc.) without an extra confirm.	
--no-preview is a footgun outside of well-tested pipelines. The
preview is the only thing standing between you and an unintended
delete.
data.diff#diff:
$ lithos diff [PROJECT] --environment <label> [--live]
Print the diff between persisted state and project configuration. Useful
in pull-request CI to comment "what would this PR do?" without applying.By default diff is offline — it does not contact Roblox. Pass
--live to run the same reconciliation pass that deploy runs, surface
drift, and diff against the reconciled previous-state graph:
$ lithos diff --environment dev --live
Use --live when you suspect drift; use plain diff when you just want
to know what your YAML changes would do.
data.undo#undo:
$ lithos undo [PROJECT] --environment <label> [flags]
Best-effort rollback to the most recent checkpoint Lithos recorded for an
environment. undo does not read old YAML or Git history. Instead it:
Loads the baseline snapshot stored before the last deploy or undo.
Imports the live Roblox experience so rollback plans against reality,
not stale state.
Runs the same preflight diagnostics and plan preview as deploy.
Applies the diff back toward that snapshot and records the result.
Use the same preview flags as deploy: --yes, --no-preview, and
--plain-preview. --allow-purchases is also supported in case rollback
needs to recreate a paid resource.
Roblox deploys are not transactional. undo is therefore best-effort:
it reconciles live state and then drives resources back toward the last
checkpoint Lithos recorded.
data.destroy#destroy:
$ lithos destroy [PROJECT] --environment <label> [--yes]
Remove every resource Lithos manages for an environment. Lithos cannot
hard-delete most Roblox asset types, so in practice this archives them
and clears them from state.destroy is a deploy whose diff is "delete everything." It runs the
same plan preview, the same confirmation prompt, and the same dependency
ordering. Use the same flags.
destroy is irreversible from Lithos's point of view: state is wiped.
The Roblox-side assets are archived, not gone, but recovering them and
reattaching to a fresh state requires import (experimental).
data.import#import:
$ lithos import [PROJECT] --environment <label> --target-id <experience-id>
Adopt an existing Roblox experience into a Lithos project. This is for the
case where you already have a published experience and want to start
managing it with Lithos.
import is experimental. It does not match every existing resource to a
configured one — most resources will be re-created on the next deploy.
Always test on a staging environment before importing a production
experience.
A safer pattern: build a Lithos config that mirrors your production setup,
deploy it as a staging environment to verify the diff is empty, and only
then point import at production.
data.exit-codes#Exit codes:
Code	Meaning	0	Success. Includes the case "nothing to do."	1	A user-facing failure. Bad config, auth failure, apply failure, conflicting state, etc. The error message names the cause.	2	The command was cancelled at the preview / confirmation step.	
In CI, treat any non-zero exit as fatal.

data.config-file-resolution#Config file resol:
All Lithos commands accept a PROJECT argument which tells Lithos where to look for your config file.
Lithos uses the following rules to find your config file:
If the PROJECT argument was not provided, Lithos treats the current directory as the project directory.
If the PROJECT argument was a directory, Lithos checks that directory for lithos.yml, then lithos.yaml, then lithos.json, then legacy mantle.yml, then mantle.yaml.
If the PROJECT argument was a file, Lithos uses it directly. Explicit config paths can point to either YAML or JSON files.
If multiple discovered config files are present, Lithos uses the same order: lithos.yml, then lithos.yaml, then lithos.json, then legacy mantle.yml, then mantle.yaml.
If no config file is found, Lithos exits with an error that lists those search paths in order.Lithos prefers the Lithos-named files when both Lithos and Mantle variants are present, which lets you keep a
legacy file around during migration while silencing warnings once lithos.yml, lithos.yaml, or lithos.json exists.
data.outputs-command-defaults#Outputs command:
lithos outputs can be configured from the project file instead of requiring
the full output target on every command line.Add a top-level outputs block:
outputs:
  writeDir: src/shared/generated
  outputName: lithosOutputs
  format: luau
  robloxTs: true
{
  "outputs": {
    "writeDir": "src/shared/generated",
    "outputName": "lithosOutputs",
    "format": "luau",
    "robloxTs": true
  }
}
Or, for easier migration from tools like Asphalt, use the alias codegen
plus snake_case field names:
codegen:
  write_dir: src/shared/generated
  output_name: lithosOutputs
  format: luau
  typescript: true
{
  "codegen": {
    "write_dir": "src/shared/generated",
    "output_name": "lithosOutputs",
    "format": "luau",
    "typescript": true
  }
}
Supported properties:
path: full output file path.
writeDir + outputName: build the path from a project-relative directory and file name.
format: json, yaml, yml, lua, or luau.
robloxTs: write a .d.ts sidecar when the resolved output is Luau.
Rules to know:
Use either path or writeDir + outputName, not both.
If outputName has no extension, Lithos adds one from format.
If robloxTs / typescript is enabled and no format is set, Lithos defaults to .luau.
CLI flags such as --output, --format, and --roblox-ts override config values.
data.yaml-and-json-syntax#YAML and JSON synta:
Lithos config files can be written in either YAML or JSON. Directory auto-discovery looks for lithos.yml
, lithos.yaml, and lithos.json; the legacy fallback remains mantle.ymlandmantle.yaml`.
Config examples in this guide can be switched between YAML and JSON, and the same schema and field names apply to both.JSONC and comments are not supported.To quickly get started with YAML syntax, see "Learn YAML in Y Minutes"
or read through the examples in this guide and in the Examples
repo.
data.schemas#Schemas:
You can view the JSON schemas for the config files below (only for versions above 0.11.0). You can also use
the schema to add autocomplete and validation while editing either YAML or JSON config files. For VS Code,
install the YAML extension for YAML
files and use the built-in JSON language support for JSON files, then add the following to your settings:

data:
Lithos is a Roblox infrastructure-as-code tool. You describe the experience
you want to exist — places, configuration, products, badges, thumbnails,
social links, spatial voice, notifications — in a YAML or JSON file, and Lithos
makes Roblox match it.If you have used Terraform, Pulumi, or AWS CDK before, the model will feel
familiar. If you have not, the rest of this page is the only mental model
you need to use Lithos productively.
data.the-three-things-lithos-owns#The three t:
A configuration file (lithos.yml or lithos.json) — the source of
truth. What you want to exist.
A state file (.lithos-state.yml, local or remote) — the current
graph Lithos believes exists, plus a short deployment history.
A live API (Roblox + Open Cloud) — what actually exists right now.
Every command is a function of those three inputs. deploy reconciles them
in that order: read config, read state, verify state against the live API,
plan a diff, apply it, write new state.
This is the most important sentence in these docs: state is what Lithos
thinks exists; the live API is what really exists. When they disagree,
Lithos calls that drift, and reconciles it before doing anything
destructive.
Lithos also stores recent deployment checkpoints in state. That history is
what powers lithos undo.
data.what-infrastructure-as-code-buys-you#Wha:
You probably already have a game.rbxlx in source control. Lithos extends
that idea to the surrounding metadata that today lives in Studio dialogs and
the Creator Hub: place names, server sizes, products, passes, badges,
thumbnails, social links, voice settings. All of it becomes a code review,
not a click-through.The practical consequence:
Every deploy is reviewable: a plan preview shows exactly which fields
on which resources will change, before any byte hits Roblox.
Every change is rollback-able: revert the YAML and redeploy when you are
intentionally changing desired state, or run lithos undo to drive Roblox
back to the last recorded checkpoint.
Every environment is reproducible: dev and prod come from the same
config with declarative overrides, not parallel checklists.
Every CI pipeline is boring: a single binary, a state file in S3 or
R2, and three secrets.
data.what-lithos-is-not#What Lithos is not:
Not a replacement for Rojo. Rojo turns Lua
source files into a .rbxlx. Lithos uploads that .rbxlx to a place and
configures everything around it. They are complementary tools.
Not a runtime. Lithos runs on your machine or in CI. It does not run
inside Roblox.
Not an SDK. There is no Lithos library you call from your game code.
data.where-to-go-next#Where to go next:
Getting Started — install the tool and
deploy a real example end-to-end.
The resource graph — how Lithos
decides what to create, update, and destroy.
State and reconciliation — how state files
work and what happens when they go stale.
Environments — how dev and prod
share a single config.
If you are coming from Mantle, read Migrating from Mantle first.
